items.q: Find the pH of Solution A from its measured hydronium concentration.

mistakes.why: Value: that is the pOH. pH = −log[H₃O⁺] uses the hydronium concentration you were given directly.
Value: you used ln. pH is defined with the base-10 log: pH = −log[H₃O⁺].

items.q: What is the pH of Solution B?

mistakes.why: Value: that is the pOH, −log[OH⁻]. Subtract it from 14.00 to get the pH.

items.q: What is [H₃O⁺] in Solution C, in mol/L? Give your answer in scientific notation.

mistakes.why: Value: that is [OH⁻], 10^−pOH. For hydronium use [H₃O⁺] = 10^−pH = 10^−9.15.

items.q: Which solution has the highest concentration of H₃O⁺?
options: Solution D, with a pOH of 11.62
Solution A, with [H₃O⁺] = 3.2 × 10⁻⁴ M
Solution B, with [OH⁻] = 2.5 × 10⁻³ M
Solution C, with a pH of 9.15

items.q: About how many times greater is [H₃O⁺] in Solution D than in Solution A?
options: About 13 times
About 1.5 times
About 1.1 times
About 129 times

items.q: Which box represents a basic solution?
options: Box 3
Box 1
Box 2
Box 4

items.q: In Boxes 1, 2 and 3 the product (number of H₃O⁺) × (number of OH⁻) is the same. What does this show?
options: [H₃O⁺][OH⁻] is fixed at a given temperature, so raising one lowers the other
Each solution contains the same total number of ions
Adding acid to water adds OH⁻ ions as well as H₃O⁺ ions
The pH of each of the three solutions is the same

items.q: Box 1 and Box 4 are both pure water. Which statement about Box 4 is best supported?
options: It is warmer than Box 1, because the ionization of water is endothermic
It is cooler than Box 1, because cold water holds more ions
It is acidic, because it contains more H₃O⁺ than Box 1
It has a higher pH than Box 1, because it contains more OH⁻

items.q: Suppose Box 1 is pure water at 25 °C, so [H₃O⁺] = 1.0 × 10⁻⁷ M. Box 2 has the same volume. What is the pH of Box 2?

mistakes.why: Value: Box 2 has 4 hydronium ions, but Box 1 already has 2. The concentration is twice Box 1, not four times.

items.q: What is the pH of pure water at 50 °C?

mistakes.why: Value: 7.00 is neutral only at 25 °C. At 50 °C, [H₃O⁺] = √Kw, and Kw is larger.
Value: you took −log Kw. In pure water [H₃O⁺] = [OH⁻], so [H₃O⁺] = √Kw: take the square root first.

items.q: A student measures pure water at 50 °C and reads pH 6.63. Which claim is correct?
options: The water is neutral, because [H₃O⁺] still equals [OH⁻]
The water is acidic, because its pH is below 7
The water is acidic, because heating drives off the OH⁻ ions
The pH meter is faulty, because pure water reads 7.00

items.q: What does the trend in Kw with temperature show about the reaction 2 H₂O(l) ⇌ H₃O⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq)?
options: It is endothermic: heating favors the forward reaction
It is exothermic: heating favors the forward reaction
It is endothermic: heating favors the reverse reaction
It goes to completion at 50 °C

items.q: A sample of pure water is cooled from 25 °C to 0 °C. Predict the change in each quantity.
A solution at 25 °C has [H₃O⁺] = 4.0 × 10⁻³ M. What is [OH⁻]? Include the unit.

mistakes.why: Value: you divided [H₃O⁺] by Kw. Rearrange Kw = [H₃O⁺][OH⁻] to [OH⁻] = Kw / [H₃O⁺].

items.q: Solution P has pH 4.0 and Solution Q has pH 6.0. How does [H₃O⁺] in P compare with Q?
options: 100 times greater in P
2 times greater in P
1.5 times greater in P
100 times smaller in P

items.q: Put the steps for finding the pH of a 25 °C solution from its [OH⁻] in order.
options: Take −log[OH⁻] to get the pOH
Subtract the pOH from 14.00
Round the pH to as many decimal places as [OH⁻] has significant figures
Check: a basic solution should give a pH above 7

items.q: A solution has [H₃O⁺] = 0.0050 M. How should its pH be reported?
A solution at 25 °C has pH 8.25. What is its pOH?

mistakes.why: Value: you added the pH to 14.00. pH + pOH = 14.00, so pOH = 14.00 − pH.

items.q: Which statements are true for every aqueous solution at 25 °C? Select all that apply.
options: A solution with pH 9 contains no H₃O⁺ ions
pH + pOH = 14.00
Adding OH⁻ raises [H₃O⁺]
An acidic solution contains no OH⁻ ions

items.q: What is the pH of Bottle 1?

mistakes.why: Value: that is the pOH. HNO₃ gives H₃O⁺ directly, so pH = −log(0.0250).

items.q: What is the pH of Bottle 2?

mistakes.why: Value: each Ba(OH)₂ gives two OH⁻ ions, so [OH⁻] = 2 × 0.0150 = 0.0300 M.
Value: that is the pOH. Subtract it from 14.00 to get the pH.

items.q: Which bottle has the highest pH?
options: Bottle 2
Bottle 3
Bottle 4
Bottle 1

items.q: What is the pH of Bottle 4? (Hint: water itself also supplies H₃O⁺.)

mistakes.why: Value: an acid cannot make water basic. At 1.0 × 10⁻⁸ M the acid adds less H₃O⁺ than water already has, so the pH stays just below 7.

items.q: A student dilutes 10.0 mL of Bottle 1 to 100.0 mL with water. What happens to the pH?
options: It rises by 1.00 unit
It falls by 1.00 unit
It rises by 10 units
It stays the same, because the moles of acid are unchanged

items.q: How many moles of H₃O⁺ are left over after the reaction?

mistakes.why: Value: that is the H₃O⁺ before mixing. The 0.00225 mol of OH⁻ added reacts with it one to one; subtract.

items.q: What is the pH of the mixture?

mistakes.why: Value: you divided by the acid volume only. After mixing, the H₃O⁺ is spread through the total volume, 40.0 mL.
Value: you skipped the neutralization. Subtract the moles of OH⁻ added before finding [H₃O⁺].

items.q: What total volume of 0.150 M NaOH would have to be added to the original HCl to reach the equivalence point?
At the equivalence point of this mixture, what is the pH and why?
options: 7.00, because Na⁺ and Cl⁻ do not react with water
Below 7, because HCl was in the flask first
Above 7, because NaOH was added last
7.00, because no ions are left in the flask

items.q: Which box cannot represent a real mixture, and why?
options: Z, because H₃O⁺ and OH⁻ would react until one of them was nearly gone
X, because a solution needs H₃O⁺ ions to conduct electricity
Y, because there are more Na⁺ ions than Cl⁻ ions
W, because there are more Cl⁻ ions than Na⁺ ions

items.q: Which box has the highest pH?
options: Y
X
W

items.q: Each ion drawn in Box Y stands for 1.0 × 10⁻³ mol, and the box holds 0.50 L. What is the pH of the mixture?

mistakes.why: Value: that is the pOH. Box Y is basic, so pH = 14.00 − pOH.
Value: you used moles as if they were molarity. Divide 2.0 × 10⁻³ mol by 0.50 L first.

items.q: Which of these are strong acids in water? Select all that apply.
options: HBr
HF
HNO₂
H₂CO₃
CH₃COOH

items.q: What is the pH of 2.5 × 10⁻⁴ M Sr(OH)₂ at 25 °C?

mistakes.why: Value: Sr(OH)₂ gives two OH⁻ per formula unit; double the concentration.
Value: that is the pOH; subtract from 14.00.

items.q: A student pipets 35.0 mL of 0.200 M HCl into a 500.0 mL volumetric flask and dilutes to the mark. What is the pH of the diluted solution?

mistakes.why: Value: that is the pH before dilution. Find the new concentration with M₁V₁ = M₂V₂ first.
Value: "dilute to the mark" makes the total volume 500.0 mL; do not add the 35.0 mL on top.

items.q: Solutions of 0.10 M HCl and 0.10 M HNO₃ have the same pH, even though the acids are different. Which explanation is best?
options: Both ionize fully, so each gives 0.10 M H₃O⁺
Both have the same molar mass, so equal moles dissolve
Cl and N have the same electronegativity, so the H–X bonds are alike
Both are diatomic, so they release the same number of protons

items.q: What is the pH after 30.0 mL of 0.0800 M KOH is added to 20.0 mL of 0.100 M HBr?

mistakes.why: Value: that is the pOH. The base is in excess, so pH = 14.00 − pOH.
Value: divide the leftover OH⁻ by the total volume, 50.0 mL, not the base volume.

items.q: Put the steps for finding the pH after mixing a strong acid with a strong base in order.
options: Find the moles of H₃O⁺ and of OH⁻ from volume × molarity
Subtract: the smaller amount is used up, the excess remains
Divide the excess by the total volume of the mixture
Convert to pH (through pOH if OH⁻ is in excess)

items.q: What is the pH of 0.20 M acetic acid?

mistakes.why: Value: you treated acetic acid as strong. Only a small fraction ionizes; set up Ka = x² / (0.20 − x).
Value: you forgot the square root. Ka = x²/C, so x = √(Ka × C).

items.q: For 0.10 M solutions of each acid, which has the highest pH?
options: Hypochlorous acid
Hydrofluoric acid
Nitrous acid
Acetic acid

items.q: What is the percent ionization of 0.050 M HNO₂? (Check whether the small-x assumption is valid.)

mistakes.why: Value: the small-x shortcut is off by more than 5% here. Solve the quadratic x² + Ka·x − Ka·C = 0.

items.q: What is Kb for the fluoride ion, F⁻? Give your answer in scientific notation.

mistakes.why: Value: Kb is not 1/Ka. For a conjugate pair Ka × Kb = Kw, so Kb = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ / Ka.
Value: you divided Ka by Kw. Rearrange Ka × Kb = Kw to Kb = Kw / Ka.

items.q: Which of the four conjugate bases, OCl⁻, CH₃COO⁻, NO₂⁻ and F⁻, is the strongest base?
options: OCl⁻
F⁻
NO₂⁻
CH₃COO⁻

options: Box 2
Box 1
Box 3

items.q: Boxes 1 and 3 contain the same acid at the same temperature. Which statement is best supported?
options: Box 3 is the more dilute solution, and a larger fraction of its acid is ionized
Box 3 has the larger Ka, because a larger fraction of its acid is ionized
Box 3 has the lower pH, because a larger fraction of its acid is ionized
Both boxes have the same percent ionization, because they hold the same acid

items.q: Treat Box 1 as an equilibrium mixture in which each particle drawn stands for 0.010 mol in 1.0 L. What is Ka for this acid?
Which statements about Box 1 are true? Select all that apply.
options: [HA] is greater than [A⁻]
[H₃O⁺] equals the starting concentration of the acid
The acid is mostly un-ionized
Adding water would lower its percent ionization

items.q: What is [OH⁻] in the solution? Include the unit.

mistakes.why: Value: ammonia is a weak base; only a small fraction reacts. Use Kb = x² / (0.15 − x).
Value: take the square root: x² = Kb × C.

items.q: What is the pH of the ammonia cleaning solution?

mistakes.why: Value: that is the pOH. The solution is basic: pH = 14.00 − pOH.
Value: you treated NH₃ as a strong base. Only about 1% of it reacts with water.

items.q: What is the pKa of NH₄⁺, the conjugate acid of ammonia?

mistakes.why: Value: that is pKb of NH₃. For the conjugate acid, pKa = 14.00 − pKb.

items.q: A student says, "Ammonia is a weak base, so its solution must be close to neutral." Which response is best?
options: "Weak" means only a small fraction reacts, but 0.15 M NH₃ still makes enough OH⁻ to give pH 11.2
"Weak" means the solution is dilute, so the pH is close to 7
Weak bases make H₃O⁺ instead of OH⁻, so the pH is below 7
Weak bases react fully with water, so the pH is very high

items.q: A 0.085 M solution of a weak acid HA has pH 3.25. What is Ka? Give your answer in scientific notation.

mistakes.why: Value: square [H₃O⁺]. Both H₃O⁺ and A⁻ are in the numerator, and they are equal: Ka = x² / (C − x).

items.q: Put the steps for finding the pH of a weak acid solution from Ka and its concentration in order.
options: Write the ionization equation and the Ka expression
Set up an ICE table: change −x for HA, +x for H₃O⁺ and A⁻
Assume x is small and solve x = √(Ka × C)
Check that x is under 5% of C (otherwise solve the quadratic)
pH = −log x

items.q: Solution 1 is 0.10 M HCl and Solution 2 is 0.10 M HF. Each is diluted tenfold. How do their pH values change?
options: HCl rises by 1.0 unit; HF rises by less than 1.0 unit
Both rise by exactly 1.0 unit
HCl rises by 1.0 unit; HF rises by more than 1.0 unit
Neither changes, because Ka and Kw do not change

items.q: Which claim correctly explains why acetic acid is classified as a weak acid?
options: Ka is much less than 1, so at equilibrium most acetic acid molecules are un-ionized
Its solutions have a pH above 7
Each acetic acid molecule has one ionizable hydrogen
Its solutions are usually dilute

items.q: What is the pH of 0.25 M NaOCl? (Ka of HOCl = 3.0 × 10⁻⁸.)

mistakes.why: Value: OCl⁻ is a base, not an acid. Find Kb = Kw/Ka and solve for [OH⁻].
Value: that is the pOH. Subtract it from 14.00.

mistakes.why: Value: that is the pH of the acid alone. Let the 2.50 × 10⁻³ mol OH⁻ react with the acid first.

mistakes.why: Value: 7.00 is the equivalence pH only for a strong acid with a strong base. Here acetate, a weak base, is left in solution.
Value: the volume doubled to 100.0 mL, so [CH₃COO⁻] = 0.0500 M, not 0.100 M.

items.q: What is the pH in Flask 4?

mistakes.why: Value: divide the excess OH⁻ by the total volume, 110.0 mL, not the 60.0 mL of base.

It has more Cl⁻ than H₃O⁺, and a buffer needs equal amounts

items.q: Which is the net ionic equation for Reaction I?
options: HF(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → F⁻(aq) + H₂O(l)
H₃O⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → 2 H₂O(l)
HF(aq) + NaOH(aq) → NaF(aq) + H₂O(l)
H⁺(aq) + F⁻(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → F⁻(aq) + H₂O(l)

items.q: What is K for the net reaction HF(aq) + OH⁻(aq) ⇌ F⁻(aq) + H₂O(l)? Give your answer in scientific notation.

mistakes.why: Value: this reaction is HF ionizing (Ka) plus the reverse of water ionizing (1/Kw). Multiply Ka by 1/Kw: K = Ka / Kw.
Value: that is Kb of F⁻, the reverse of this reaction. Here K = Ka / Kw = 1/Kb.

items.q: Equal moles of NH₃ and HCl react in Reaction II. Which describes the final solution?
options: Acidic, because NH₄⁺ gives protons to water
Neutral, because equal moles of acid and base reacted
Basic, because NH₃ is a base
Neutral, because Cl⁻ is a spectator ion

items.q: In Reaction II, a small amount of HCl (less than the moles of NH₃) is added to an NH₃ solution. Predict the change in each quantity.
A solution contains 0.30 M HNO₂ and 0.20 M NaNO₂ (Ka of HNO₂ = 4.0 × 10⁻⁴). What is its pH?
